cards.front: What are the 6 Ps of compartment syndrome?
cards.back:
Pain out of proportion, Pain worse with passive stretch, Paresthesia/hypoesthesia, Pallor, Polar (cold), Pulse discrepancies

The 6 Ps indicate advanced compartment syndrome - do not wait for all to be present before treating.

cards.front: What nerve injuries are at risk with anterior shoulder dislocation?
cards.back:
Axillary nerve (lateral aspect of shoulder) and Musculocutaneous nerve (extensor aspect of forearm)

These nerves are vulnerable during dislocation and reduction maneuvers.

cards.front: What are 'The 6 Ps' of compartment syndrome?
cards.back:
Pain out of proportion, Pain worse with passive stretch, Paresthesia/hypoesthesia, Pallor, Polar (cold), Paralysis

The 6 Ps are clinical signs of compartment syndrome; however, presence of any indicates advanced disease as capillary perfusion pressure is only 30 mmHg.

cards.front: What nerves are at risk in anterior shoulder dislocation?
cards.back:
Axillary nerve (lateral aspect of shoulder) and musculocutaneous nerve (extensor aspect of forearm)

These nerves are commonly injured in shoulder dislocations and should be assessed as part of the neurovascular examination.

cards.front: What imaging view confirms anterior shoulder dislocation?
cards.back:
Lateral view showing humeral head anterior to glenoid

The lateral view is essential for confirming dislocation direction and guiding reduction technique.

cards.front: What is the immobilization position after anterior shoulder dislocation reduction?
cards.back:
Internal rotation

Immobilization in internal rotation helps maintain reduction and allows soft tissue healing.

cards.front: What is the most common direction of shoulder dislocation and what is the recurrence rate for patients under 20 years old?
cards.back:
Anterior dislocation accounts for >90% of shoulder dislocations. Recurrence rate for patients <20 years old is 65-95%.

Anterior dislocations are far more common than posterior (5%). Young patients have the highest recurrence rate because of increased activity levels and possible structural predisposition. Recurrence rate decreases with age: 60-70% for 20-40 yr, 2-4% for >40 yr.

cards.front: Name the four rotator cuff muscles (SITS) and their primary actions.
cards.back:
Supraspinatus (abduction), Infraspinatus (external rotation), Teres Minor (external rotation), Subscapularis (internal rotation and adduction).

The SITS muscles stabilize the humeral head in the glenoid fossa. Supraspinatus is most commonly injured due to impingement under the acromion. All attach to the greater tuberosity except subscapularis, which attaches to the lesser tuberosity.

cards.front: What does a positive Jobe's (Empty Can) test indicate, and how is it performed?
cards.back:
It suggests a supraspinatus tear. The shoulder is placed in 90° abduction, 30° horizontal flexion with internal rotation (thumb pointing down), and the patient resists downward pressure.

This test isolates the supraspinatus by placing it in a mechanically disadvantaged position. Weakness with active resistance suggests a supraspinatus tear. Impingement tests (Neer's, Hawkins-Kennedy) assess for impingement syndrome rather than a specific tear.

cards.front: What is the Rockwood classification for AC joint separation, and which grades typically require surgery?
cards.back:
Grades I-III are typically managed non-operatively (with III being operative if labourer/high-level athlete). Grades IV-VI require operative management. Classification is based on AC and CC ligament integrity.

Grade I = AC sprain, Grade II = AC torn/CC sprained, Grade III = both torn but reducible, Grades IV-VI = both torn and irreducible with varying directions of clavicle displacement. The piano key sign is a palpable step deformity seen with dislocation.

cards.front: What is the most common site of clavicle fracture and its most common mechanism of injury?
cards.back:
Middle third (80%) is the most common site. Fall on shoulder (87%) is the most common mechanism.

The middle third is the thinnest portion and most vulnerable to fracture. Clavicle fractures are common in children and unite rapidly. The most common complication is a cosmetic bump. ORIF is considered when fracture is shortened >2 cm or when distal third fracture is displaced.

cards.front: What are the three stages of adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder) and their durations?
cards.back:
1. Freezing phase (gradual onset of diffuse pain): 6-9 months. 2. Frozen phase (decreased ROM impacts function): 4-9 months. 3. Thawing phase (gradual improvement in ROM): 4-12 months.

Adhesive capsulitis usually resolves spontaneously within 18 months. Key features include restricted active AND passive ROM, night pain, and association with diabetes (5%), prolonged immobilization, and female gender. Treatment includes physiotherapy, NSAIDs, steroid injections, and manipulation under anesthesia if refractory.

cards.front: How are proximal humeral fractures classified using the Neer system, and how are the majority treated?
cards.back:
Neer classification uses 4 fracture parts (anatomic neck, surgical neck, greater tuberosity, lesser tuberosity). A part is displaced if angulation >45° or displacement >1 cm. 85% of proximal humeral fractures are non-displaced/minimally displaced and treated non-operatively with sling and early ROM within 14 days.

The Neer system counts displaced fracture parts, not fracture lines. Complications include AVN (especially with anatomic neck fractures), axillary nerve palsy (45%), and frozen shoulder. Hemiarthroplasty or reverse total shoulder arthroplasty may be needed in elderly patients with 4-part fractures.

cards.front: What nerve is most commonly injured with humeral shaft fractures, and at what location?
cards.back:
The radial nerve, particularly with Holstein-Lewis distal 1/3 humeral shaft fractures. Most cases recover spontaneously in 3-4 months.

The radial nerve courses in the spiral groove of the humerus. Injury manifests as wrist drop and sensory loss over the dorsal hand. Radial nerve function must be tested before and after treatment. EMG is performed if no recovery by 3-4 months.

cards.front: What is a Monteggia fracture and how does it differ from a Galeazzi fracture?
cards.back:
Monteggia: fracture of proximal ulna with radial head dislocation. Galeazzi: fracture of distal radial shaft with DRUJ disruption. Mnemonic: Monteggia = Ulnar fracture, Galeazzi = Radial fracture.

For Monteggia fractures, always assess proximal radius in all isolated ulna fractures. The most common nerve injury is PIN. Galeazzi is called the 'fracture of necessity' because all cases require operative management (ORIF of radius).

cards.front: Describe the Colles' fracture and its classic deformity.
cards.back:
Extra-articular transverse distal radius fracture (~2 cm proximal to radiocarpal joint) with dorsal displacement + ulnar styloid fracture. Classic 'dinner fork' deformity.

Colles' fracture is the most common fracture in those >40 yr, caused by FOOSH. Treatment goals: restore radial height (13 mm), radial inclination (23°), and volar tilt (11°). Smith's fracture is the reverse (volar displacement, 'garden spade' deformity) caused by fall on flexed hand.

cards.front: Why is a scaphoid fracture particularly at risk for AVN, and how should a suspected scaphoid fracture with negative initial x-ray be managed?
cards.back:
The proximal pole receives up to 100% of its arterial blood supply from the radial artery entering at the distal pole. A proximal fracture disrupts this retrograde blood supply. If x-ray is negative but clinical suspicion is high (snuff box tenderness), treat as positive with thumb spica cast and repeat x-ray in 2 weeks; if still negative, order CT or MRI.

Proximal pole fractures have the highest AVN rate (up to 100% for proximal fifth). Waist fractures heal 80-90% of the time. Non-union is the most common complication. SNAC (scaphoid nonunion advanced collapse) can cause chronic wrist arthritis.

cards.front: What are the cervical nerve root levels for key motor functions: deltoid, biceps, triceps, and interossei?
cards.back:
C5: deltoid and biceps. C6: biceps and brachioradialis. C7: triceps, wrist flexion, finger extension. C8: interossei, digital flexors.

Key reflexes mirror these: C5/6 = biceps, C6 = brachioradialis, C7 = triceps, C8 = finger jerk. Radiculopathy involves impingement of a nerve root, while myelopathy involves impingement of the spinal cord. In the cervical spine, nerve roots exit above the corresponding vertebra.

cards.front: How do you differentiate neurogenic claudication from vascular claudication?
cards.back:
Neurogenic: aggravated by standing/walking with variable walking distance, relieved by change in position (usually flexion), relief in ~10 min. Vascular: aggravated by walking/exercise with reproducible distance, relieved by stopping activity, relief in ~2 min.

Neurogenic claudication is position-dependent (spinal stenosis), while vascular claudication is exercise-dependent (peripheral arterial disease). Neurogenic claudication is bilateral and associated with spinal stenosis, treated with flexion exercises and decompressive surgery if refractory.

cards.front: What are the red flags for back pain that warrant urgent investigation?
cards.back:
Bowel or bladder dysfunction, constitutional symptoms/malignancy, chronic disease, age >50 yr, IV drug use, neuromotor deficits.

Cauda equina syndrome (bowel/bladder dysfunction, saddle anesthesia) is a surgical emergency. Ruptured aortic aneurysm is another cause of low back pain considered a surgical emergency. Imaging is indicated if symptoms persist >6 weeks or red flags are present.

cards.front: What is the most common level for lumbar disc herniation and what nerve root is affected by an L4-5 disc herniation?
cards.back:
Most common level: L5-S1 > L4-5 > L3-4. An L4-5 disc herniation typically compresses the L5 nerve root (posterolateral herniation compresses the traversing root).

L5 radiculopathy presents with weakness of extensor hallucis longus, sensory loss in the 1st dorsal webspace, and is screened by heel walking. 90% of patients improve in 3 months with non-operative treatment. Surgical discectomy is indicated for progressive neurological deficit or cauda equina syndrome.

cards.front: What is the most life-threatening complication of pelvic fractures and what is the initial emergency management?
cards.back:
Hemorrhage is the most life-threatening complication. Initial management includes IV fluids/blood, pelvic binder/sheet, and consideration of external fixation vs. emergent angiography/embolization.

Pelvic fractures are classified by the Tile system into stable (A), rotationally unstable (B), and rotationally + vertically unstable (C). Always assess for genitourinary injury. Open pelvic fractures include those with involvement of rectum or urogenital structures. FAST/DPL may indicate need for laparotomy.

cards.front: How does the clinical presentation differ between anterior and posterior hip dislocations?
cards.back:
Anterior: shortened, abducted, externally rotated limb. Posterior: shortened, adducted, internally rotated limb. Posterior is most common (90%).

Posterior dislocations typically result from a dashboard injury (axial load to knee with hip flexed and adducted). On x-ray, the affected femoral head appears smaller. Hip dislocations must be reduced within 6 hours to decrease risk of AVN. Sciatic nerve palsy occurs in 25% of posterior dislocations.

cards.front: What is the Garden classification of femoral neck fractures and how does it guide treatment?
cards.back:
Types I-II (non-displaced): internal fixation to prevent displacement. Types III-IV (displaced): young patients get ORIF; elderly patients get hemi- or total hip arthroplasty.

Garden classification: I = incomplete/valgus impacted, II = complete/non-displaced, III = partially displaced/varus, IV = completely displaced. The femoral head blood supply (medial and lateral femoral circumflex arteries) is at risk of disruption with displaced fractures, leading to AVN.

cards.front: What are the x-ray findings of osteoarthritis (mnemonic LOSS)?
cards.back:
L = Loss of joint space, O = Osteophytes, S = Subchondral sclerosis, S = Subchondral cysts.

OA findings on x-ray contrast with inflammatory arthritis (RA), which shows periarticular osteopenia, periarticular erosions, and concentric joint space narrowing. Treatment of hip/knee OA progresses from exercise and acetaminophen to NSAIDs to intra-articular injections to arthroplasty.

cards.front: What is the Lachman test and what does it assess?
cards.back:
It assesses ACL integrity. With the knee in 20-30° flexion, stabilize the distal femur and attempt to sublux the tibia anteriorly. Positive test = increased anterior tibial translation. It has the highest diagnostic accuracy for ACL tears (positive LR 25.0, negative LR 0.1).

The Lachman test is more reliable than the anterior drawer test because less muscular stabilization occurs at 20-30° flexion. The pivot shift test also assesses ACL integrity. ACL tears commonly occur with non-contact deceleration injuries, present with an audible 'pop' and immediate swelling.

cards.front: What is the O'Donoghue's 'unhappy triad' of the knee?
cards.back:
ACL tear + MCL tear + meniscal damage (medial and/or lateral).

This triad typically occurs from a valgus force to the knee with external rotation. MCL tears present with tenderness above and below the medial joint line and laxity with valgus stress. A locked knee (inability to fully extend due to mechanical block) from a meniscal tear is a surgical emergency.

cards.front: What is the Salter-Harris classification and which types are most likely to cause growth arrest?
cards.back:
S = Straight through (Type I, through growth plate), A = Above (Type II, through metaphysis), L = beLow (Type III, through epiphysis), T = Through (Type IV, through both), R = Ram/crush (Type V). Types III-V are most likely to cause growth arrest.

Type II is the most common Salter-Harris fracture. Types I and II generally heal well with closed reduction. Types III-V require anatomic reduction (often ORIF) and carry higher risk of growth arrest and progressive deformity. In children, growth plate is weaker than ligaments.

cards.front: What is SCFE, who is most at risk, and what is the treatment?
cards.back:
Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis: Type I Salter-Harris injury at the proximal hip with displacement of the metaphysis. Most common in obese adolescent males during pubertal growth spurt. Treatment: operative percutaneous in-situ fixation without reduction.

SCFE presents with groin/thigh/knee pain, limp, restricted internal rotation, and obligatory external rotation with passive flexion (Drehmann sign). Klein's line on AP x-ray should cross femoral epiphysis. Stable SCFE has <10% risk of osteonecrosis; unstable has 24-47% risk. Bilateral involvement occurs in ~25%.

cards.front: What are the clinical features of developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) and the key physical exam tests?
cards.back:
Limited hip abduction (<60°), leg length discrepancy, asymmetric skin folds. Barlow's test: flex hips/knees, adduct and push posteriorly to dislocate (tests if hip is dislocatable). Ortolani's test: abduct hip with fingertips to reduce (positive = palpable clunk if hip is reducible).

DDH is the most common orthopedic disorder in newborns. Risk factors: 5 Fs = Family history, Female, First-born, Foot-first (breech), Left hip. Screening U/S at 4-6 weeks if risk factors. Treatment: 0-6 mo Pavlik harness; 6-18 mo GA reduction + spica cast; >18 mo open reduction.

cards.front: What is Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease and what is its prognosis?
cards.back:
Idiopathic AVN of the femoral head presenting at 4-8 years. M:F = 5:1. Child presents with limp, hip/groin/knee pain, decreased internal rotation and abduction. Prognosis is better in males, age <6, <50% femoral head involvement, and abduction >30°.

Goal of treatment is to keep the femoral head contained in the acetabulum and maintain ROM. 60% of involved hips do not require operative intervention. Natural history is early onset OA and decreased ROM. X-ray shows eventual collapse of femoral head. MRI or bone scan needed if x-ray initially negative.

cards.front: What is the Thompson test and what does it assess?
cards.back:
With patient prone, squeeze the calf. Normal response: passive plantarflexion. Positive test (no plantarflexion) indicates Achilles tendon rupture.

Achilles tendon rupture most commonly occurs 2-6 cm from its insertion where blood supply is poorest. Risk factors include chronic tendonitis, steroid injections, and fluoroquinolone antibiotics. Level 1 evidence suggests no difference in re-rupture rates between operative and non-operative management with functional rehabilitation.

cards.front: What are the features of a Codman's triangle on x-ray and what does it indicate?
cards.back:
A triangular area of periosteal elevation where the partially ossified periosteum is lifted off the cortex by neoplastic tissue. It indicates a malignant bone lesion.

Other radiographic features of malignant bone tumours include: 'onion skin' or 'sunburst' periosteal reaction, poorly defined borders with wide zone of transition, cortical destruction, and soft tissue mass. Benign lesions have well-demarcated borders, narrow zone of transition, and no periosteal reaction.

cards.front: What are the Danis-Weber classification types for ankle fractures and their management?
cards.back:
Type A (infra-syndesmotic): syndesmosis intact, non-operative. Type B (trans-syndesmotic): most common, some need ORIF. Type C (supra-syndesmotic): frequently tears syndesmosis, all need ORIF.

Classification is based on level of fibular fracture relative to syndesmosis. Operative indications include fracture-dislocation, any talar displacement, displaced medial/lateral malleolar fracture, trimalleolar fractures, and persistent medial clear space widening.

cards.front: What is scoliosis, how is it measured, and when is surgical intervention indicated?
cards.back:
Lateral curvature of spine with vertebral rotation, measured by Cobb angle. Treatment: <25° observe; >25° or progressive: bracing; >45° or cosmetically unacceptable or respiratory problems: surgical correction (spinal fusion).

Idiopathic scoliosis (90% of cases) most commonly presents at 10-14 years and is more frequent and severe in females. Adams forward bend test reveals thoracic/lumbar prominence. Scoliosis screening is not recommended in Canada. Bracing halts/slows progression but does not reverse deformity.

cards.front: What are the motor and sensory functions of the axillary nerve, and what nerve roots does it arise from?
cards.back:
Motor: deltoid, teres minor, triceps (long head). Sensory: lateral upper arm ('Sergeant's Patch'). Nerve roots: C5, C6.

The axillary nerve arises from the posterior cord of the brachial plexus (C5-C6). It is commonly injured in shoulder dislocations and proximal humerus fractures, causing deltoid weakness and sensory loss over the lateral upper arm.

cards.front: What are the motor and sensory functions of the radial nerve, and what nerve roots does it arise from?
cards.back:
Motor: triceps (medial and lateral heads), forearm supination, wrist/thumb/finger extensors, wrist abductors. Sensory: lateral dorsum of the hand, medial upper forearm. Nerve roots: C5, C6, C7, C8.

The radial nerve is the most commonly injured nerve in the upper extremity. Wrist drop (loss of wrist extension) is the classic presentation. Injury commonly occurs with midshaft humerus fractures.

cards.front: What are the motor and sensory functions of the median nerve, and what nerve roots does it arise from?
cards.back:
Motor: forearm pronation, wrist flexors, flexion of 1st–3rd digits, thumb opposition. Sensory: palmar thumb to radial half of 4th digit, and dorsal tips of digits 1 to radial half of digit 4. Nerve roots: C6, C7.

The median nerve is tested with the 'OK Sign' (AIN branch). It can be injured at the wrist (carpal tunnel syndrome) causing thenar wasting and loss of opposition. AIN injury causes loss of pinch (index finger FDP + FPL).

cards.front: What are the motor and sensory functions of the ulnar nerve, and what nerve roots does it arise from?
cards.back:
Motor: wrist flexors and adductors, flexion of 4th–5th digits, finger abduction/adduction. Sensory: medial palm and dorsum of hand, 5th digit and medial half of 4th digit. Nerve roots: C8, T1.

The ulnar nerve is tested by asking the patient to 'spread fingers.' It is commonly injured at the medial epicondyle (cubital tunnel) causing a 'claw hand' deformity of the 4th and 5th digits and hypothenar wasting.

cards.front: What are the motor and sensory functions of the tibial nerve, and what nerve roots does it arise from?
cards.back:
Motor: ankle plantar flexion, knee flexion, great toe flexion. Sensory: sole of foot. Nerve roots: L5, S1.

The tibial nerve supplies the posterior compartment of the leg and the plantar surface of the foot. It runs through the tarsal tunnel on the medial side of the ankle and can be compressed there (tarsal tunnel syndrome).

cards.front: What is the difference in motor function and sensory territory between the superficial peroneal nerve and the deep peroneal nerve?
cards.back:
Superficial peroneal: ankle eversion, dorsum of foot (sensory). Deep peroneal: ankle dorsiflexion/inversion and great toe extension, 1st web space (sensory). Both arise from L5, S1.

Common fibular (peroneal) nerve injury (e.g., at fibular neck) causes foot drop — loss of ankle dorsiflexion (deep peroneal) and eversion (superficial peroneal). The 1st web space is the key sensory landmark for deep peroneal nerve testing.

cards.front: What muscles are in the anterior compartment of the forearm?
cards.back:
Pronator Teres, Flexor Carpi Radialis, Palmaris Longus, Flexor Carpi Ulnaris, Flexor Digitorum Superficialis, Flexor Digitorum Profundus, Flexor Pollicis Longus, Pronator Quadratus.

The anterior forearm compartment contains the forearm flexors and pronators, which are predominantly innervated by the median nerve (with FCU and FDP to digits 4-5 by the ulnar nerve). Compartment syndrome here can cause Volkmann's ischemic contracture.

cards.front: What muscles comprise the medial compartment of the thigh?
cards.back:
Adductor Longus, Adductor Brevis, Adductor Magnus, Gracilis, Pectineus.

The medial compartment of the thigh contains the hip adductors, innervated primarily by the obturator nerve (L2-L4). The pectineus is also partially innervated by the femoral nerve. These muscles are important in gait and in obturator nerve injury assessment.

cards.front: What are the key elements in describing a fracture on imaging?
cards.back:
1. Name of injured bone; 2. Integrity of skin/soft tissue (open vs. closed); 3. Location (epiphyseal, metaphyseal, diaphyseal, physis); 4. Orientation/fracture pattern (transverse, oblique, butterfly, segmental, spiral, comminuted, intra-articular, compression, torus, greenstick, pathologic); 5. Alignment of fracture fragments (non-displaced, displaced, distracted, translated, angulated, rotated, shortened, avulsion).

A systematic approach to fracture description is essential for communication and documentation. Displacement refers to the position of the distal fragment relative to the proximal. Varus angulation means the apex points away from the midline.

cards.front: What is the difference between a torus fracture and a greenstick fracture, and in what patient population are they seen?
cards.back:
Torus: compression of the bony cortex on one side while the other remains intact. Greenstick: compression of one side with fracture of the opposite cortex. Both are seen in children (paediatric population).

Paediatric bone is more pliable than adult bone, allowing these incomplete fracture patterns. Torus (buckle) fractures are often stable and treated with splinting. Greenstick fractures may require reduction if significantly angulated.

cards.front: What is a spiral fracture and what mechanism of injury produces it?
cards.back:
A spiral fracture is a complex, multi-planar fracture line resulting from a rotational (torsional) force. It is typically a low-energy injury.

Spiral fractures in children can raise concern for non-accidental trauma (NAT/child abuse), particularly when the history is inconsistent. In adults, they commonly occur in long bones due to twisting injuries (e.g., skiing).

cards.front: What does the orthopedic 'Rule of 2s' refer to in x-ray imaging?
cards.back:
2 sides (bilateral views for comparison), 2 views (AP + lateral at minimum), 2 joints (joint above and below the fracture), 2 times (before and after reduction).

The Rule of 2s ensures adequate fracture assessment and prevents missed injuries. For example, a forearm fracture should include imaging of the wrist and elbow. Post-reduction films confirm adequate alignment.

cards.front: What are the indications for open reduction of a fracture ('NO CAST' mnemonic)?
cards.back:
N – Neurovascular compromise; O – Open fracture; C – failed Closed reduction; A – unable to Apply cast or traction; S – Salter-Harris 3, 4, 5; T – pathologic fractures.

Open reduction with internal fixation (ORIF) is indicated when closed management would fail or lead to unacceptable outcomes. Displaced intra-articular fractures also require ORIF to restore joint congruity and minimize post-traumatic OA.

cards.front: Describe the timeline and stages of normal fracture healing.
cards.back:
Weeks 0–3: hematoma formation, macrophages surround fracture site. Weeks 3–6: osteoclasts remove sharp edges, callus forms within hematoma. Weeks 6–12: bone forms within callus, bridging fragments. Months 6–12: cortical gap bridged by bone. Years 1–2: normal architecture achieved through remodelling.

Fracture healing follows a predictable sequence. Factors delaying healing include infection, poor immobilization, smoking, malnutrition, and certain medications (NSAIDs, steroids). Wolff's Law states that bone adapts its mass to the degree of mechanical loading applied.

cards.front: What are the clinical and radiographic criteria for fracture union?
cards.back:
Clinical: no tenderness to palpation, no mobility at fracture site, minimal/no deformity, ability to weight bear without pain. Radiographic: trabeculae crossing fracture site, visible callus bridging site on at least 3 of 4 cortices.

Both clinical and radiographic criteria must be assessed together. Radiographic healing lags behind clinical healing. If there is clinical union without radiographic evidence, the patient may progress with weight-bearing.

cards.front: List the early and late local complications of fractures.
cards.back:
Early local: compartment syndrome, neurological injury, vascular injury, infection, implant failure, fracture blisters, CRPS (RSD). Late local: malunion/non-union, AVN, osteomyelitis, heterotopic ossification, post-traumatic OA, joint stiffness/adhesive capsulitis.

Systemic complications include sepsis, PE, ARDS secondary to fat embolism, and hemorrhagic shock. Fat embolism syndrome presents with SOB, hypoxemia, petechial rash, thrombocytopenia, and neurological symptoms — classically 24–72 h after long bone fracture.

cards.front: What is Complex Regional Pain Syndrome (CRPS/RSD), and what are its hallmarks?
cards.back:
CRPS is sustained sympathetic activity characterized by: pain out of proportion to physical exam findings, hyperalgesia, allodynia, and autonomic signs (temperature asymmetry, skin changes, sudomotor changes).

CRPS is a late complication of fractures or soft tissue injury. It is diagnosed clinically using the Budapest Criteria. Treatment includes physiotherapy, pain management, sympathetic nerve blocks, and psychological support.

cards.front: What are the properties of articular (hyaline) cartilage, and why does it have limited healing capacity?
cards.back:
Articular cartilage is a 2–4 mm avascular, aneural, and alymphatic layer covering the ends of articulating bones, providing a nearly frictionless surface. It receives nutrition from synovial fluid. Its avascular nature limits intrinsic repair capacity.

Due to avascularity, chondrocytes cannot mount a significant repair response after injury. This is why articular cartilage defects tend to progress. Treatment options include microfracture (to stimulate fibrocartilage formation), osteochondral grafting, and autologous chondrocyte implantation.

cards.front: What is the Outerbridge classification of chondral defects?
cards.back:
Grade I: Softening and swelling of cartilage. Grade II: Fragmentation and fissuring <1/2 inch in diameter. Grade III: Fragmentation and fissuring >1/2 inch in diameter. Grade IV: Erosion of cartilage down to bone.

The Outerbridge Classification is used intraoperatively to grade chondral damage. Grade IV corresponds to full-thickness cartilage loss exposing subchondral bone. Higher grades generally require more aggressive operative treatment.

cards.front: What are the non-operative and operative treatment options for articular cartilage defects?
cards.back:
Non-operative: rest, COX-2 inhibitors, NSAIDs, bracing, physiotherapy, intra-articular corticosteroids. Operative: microfracture, osteochondral grafting (autograft or allograft), autologous chondrocyte implantation (ACI).

Treatment is individualized based on patient factors (age, activity level, skeletal maturity) and defect factors (Outerbridge grade, subchondral bone involvement, defect size). Microfracture produces fibrocartilage rather than true hyaline cartilage.

cards.front: What x-ray views are required for evaluation of a suspected posterior shoulder dislocation?
cards.back:
AP, trans-scapular ('Y' view), and axillary views; or CT scan if axillary view cannot be obtained.

Posterior shoulder dislocations are missed up to 60–80% of the time on initial presentation. The axillary view is critical — it directly shows the humeral head posterior to the glenoid. AP view alone is unreliable and may appear deceptively normal.

cards.front: What specific x-ray views are recommended for suspected scaphoid fracture and scapholunate dissociation?
cards.back:
AP and lateral wrist views, plus a Clenched Fist (anteroposterior stress) view for scapholunate dissociation.

Scaphoid fractures may be occult on initial plain films; MRI or bone scan is recommended if clinical suspicion is high. The clenched fist view widens the scapholunate gap in scapholunate dissociation (>3 mm is abnormal — the 'Terry Thomas sign').

cards.front: What are the 6 orthopedic emergencies captured by the mnemonic 'VON CHOP'?
cards.back:
V – Vascular compromise; O – Open fracture; N – Neurological compromise/cauda equina; C – Compartment syndrome; H – Hip dislocation; O – Osteomyelitis/septic arthritis; P – Unstable Pelvic fracture.

These conditions require immediate recognition and intervention to prevent irreversible limb or life-threatening complications. Hip dislocations must be reduced within 6 hours to minimize the risk of avascular necrosis of the femoral head.

cards.front: What is Damage Control Orthopedics (DCO) and when is it applied?
cards.back:
DCO involves initial stabilization of fractures with external fixation in a hemodynamically unstable patient, followed by definitive fixation (IM nail or ORIF) once the patient is hemodynamically stable.

DCO limits the 'second hit' phenomenon — the systemic inflammatory response of major surgery in an already physiologically compromised patient. It is preferred over immediate definitive fixation in polytrauma patients with coagulopathy, acidosis, or hypothermia.

cards.front: What antibiotic regimen is recommended for a Gustilo Grade I open fracture?
cards.back:
First-generation cephalosporin (cefazolin 2g IV q8h) for 2 days. If penicillin/cephalosporin allergy: clindamycin 900 mg IV q8h. If MRSA positive: vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV q12h.

Gustilo Grade I: wound <1 cm with minimal contamination and simple/minimally comminuted fracture. Gram-positive coverage is sufficient. Antibiotics should be administered as early as possible following injury to reduce infection risk.

cards.front: What is the Gustilo Classification of open fractures, and what are the key features and antibiotic regimens for each grade?
cards.back:
Grade I: wound <1 cm, minimal contamination, simple fracture → cefazolin 2g IV q8h for 2d. Grade II: wound 1–10 cm, moderate contamination/soft tissue injury → as per Grade I. Grade III (wound >10 cm): IIIA: adequate soft tissue coverage → cefazolin + gentamicin/ceftriaxone for ≥3d; IIIB: periosteal stripping, bone exposure → same; IIIC: vascular injury → same; add metronidazole for soil/fecal contamination.

Any high-energy, comminuted fracture, shotgun wound, farmyard/soil/water contamination, exposure to oral flora, or fracture >8 h old is automatically classified as Grade III. Antibiotics should be started immediately upon arrival.

cards.front: What is the pathophysiology of compartment syndrome?
cards.back:
Increased intracompartmental pressure → decreased venous drainage and lymphatic drainage → transudation into surrounding tissue → intracompartmental pressure exceeds capillary perfusion pressure → muscle and nerve anoxia → acidosis → leaky basement membranes → muscle and nerve necrosis. Irreversible muscle necrosis occurs in 4–6 hours.

Compartment syndrome most commonly follows tibial shaft fractures, both-bone forearm fractures, or paediatric supracondylar humerus fractures. Extracompartmental causes include circumferential casts/burns or prolonged external compression.

cards.front: What are the clinical features (5 Ps) of compartment syndrome, and which is the most important early sign?
cards.back:
Pain out of proportion to injury (most important early symptom — not relieved by analgesics), Pain with passive stretch (most sensitive sign), Pressure (tense/swollen compartment), Paresthesia, Pallor, Paralysis. The last two Ps (Pallor and Paralysis) are late signs — do not wait for them.

In paediatric patients, the '3 As' may be more useful: increasing Anxiety, Agitation, and Analgesia requirements. Once pallor and paralysis develop, irreversible necrosis has likely occurred. Pain with passive stretch of compartment muscles is the most reliable early clinical finding.

cards.front: What compartment pressure reading indicates compartment syndrome requiring fasciotomy?
cards.back:
Absolute pressure ≥30 mmHg, OR delta pressure (diastolic blood pressure minus compartment pressure) <30 mmHg — either warrants urgent fasciotomy.

Compartment syndrome is primarily a clinical diagnosis. Pressure monitoring is indicated in unreliable patients (children, unconscious, associated peripheral nerve injury). The delta pressure threshold (<30 mmHg) is more sensitive than the absolute threshold alone.

cards.front: What is Volkmann's ischemic contracture, and what fractures are commonly associated with it?
cards.back:
Volkmann's ischemic contracture is ischemic necrosis of the forearm flexors followed by secondary fibrosis and muscle contractures, causing a claw-like deformity of the hand, wrist, and fingers. It is especially associated with supracondylar humerus fractures and both-bone forearm fractures.

Volkmann's contracture is the end-stage result of untreated or delayed-treatment compartment syndrome of the forearm. It is a late complication that is largely preventable with timely fasciotomy. Rehabilitation and surgical release may partially improve function.

cards.front: What is osteomyelitis, and what is its most common causative organism and route of spread?
cards.back:
Osteomyelitis is bone infection with progressive inflammatory destruction. The most common causative organism is Staphylococcus aureus. The most common route of spread is hematogenous.

Risk factors include recent trauma/surgery, immunocompromised state, diabetes, IV drug use, poor vascular supply, and peripheral neuropathy. Plain films are often normal for the first 10–12 days of infection. ESR and CRP are useful inflammatory markers.

cards.front: How is acute osteomyelitis treated compared to chronic osteomyelitis?
cards.back:
Acute: IV antibiotics empirically (adjusted after blood/bone cultures), surgery (I&D) for abscess or significant involvement. Chronic: surgical debridement + both local (antibiotic beads) and systemic IV antibiotics + hardware removal if present.

Antibiotic selection should target S. aureus empirically. Chronic osteomyelitis is defined by the presence of devitalized bone (sequestrum) and requires surgical debridement for cure. Local antibiotic delivery via beads maintains high local concentrations while minimizing systemic toxicity.

cards.front: What are the most common causative organisms of septic arthritis, and which organism is classically considered in sexually active adults?
cards.back:
Adults: Staphylococcus aureus (most common overall); consider coagulase-negative Staphylococcus with prosthetic joints. Sexually active adults and newborns: Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

Septic arthritis is a joint infection requiring urgent treatment to prevent progressive destruction. Gonococcal arthritis is the most common cause in sexually active young adults and typically presents as migratory polyarthralgia before settling into a monoarthritis.

cards.front: What are the synovial fluid findings in septic arthritis?
cards.back:
WBC >50,000 cells/mm³ with >90% neutrophils (PMNs), cloudy yellow fluid, protein >4.4 mg/dL, glucose <60% of blood glucose, no crystals, positive Gram stain.

Arthrocentesis is essential for diagnosis. WBC >100,000 cells/mm³ has a positive LR of 28.0 for septic arthritis. A PMN proportion >90% increases the LR by 3.4 for septic arthritis. Crystals suggest gout or pseudogout rather than infection.

cards.front: What are the 4 Kocher criteria used to distinguish septic arthritis from transient synovitis in children, and what is their predictive value?
cards.back:
1. Non-weight bearing; 2. ESR >40 mm/hr; 3. WBC >12,000 cells/mm³; 4. Fever (temperature >38.5°C). All 4 criteria positive: 99.6% predictive for septic joint.

The Kocher criteria help risk-stratify a child presenting with an irritable hip. Transient synovitis is the most common cause of acute hip pain in children and is a diagnosis of exclusion. A child with high predicted probability of septic arthritis requires urgent surgical washout.

cards.front: What is the treatment for septic arthritis?
cards.back:
IV antibiotics (empiric, adjusted based on joint aspirate culture and sensitivity results) + therapeutic joint aspiration (serially if necessary) OR arthroscopic/open irrigation and drainage.

Septic arthritis is a surgical emergency. Delay in treatment leads to irreversible cartilage destruction from enzymatic degradation by neutrophils. The hip and shoulder joints are generally treated with urgent surgical washout due to difficulty with serial aspiration.

cards.front: What are the mechanisms of anterior vs. posterior shoulder dislocation?
cards.back:
Anterior (>90%): abducted, externally rotated/hyperextended arm OR blow to posterior shoulder. Posterior (5%): the '3 Es' — Epileptic seizure, EtOH (ethanol intoxication), Electrocution; also FOOSH or adducted, internally rotated, flexed arm.

The glenohumeral joint is the most commonly dislocated joint in the body because stability is sacrificed for mobility. Anterior dislocations are far more common. Posterior dislocations are classically missed on AP x-ray alone.

cards.front: What is a Hill-Sachs lesion and a Bankart lesion, and with which type of shoulder dislocation is each associated?
cards.back:
Hill-Sachs lesion: compression fracture of the posterior humeral head from forceful impaction of an anteriorly dislocated head against the glenoid rim — associated with anterior dislocation. Bankart lesion: avulsion of the anterior glenoid labrum (with bone fragment = 'bony Bankart') — associated with anterior dislocation. Reverse Hill-Sachs: divot in anterior humeral head — posterior dislocation. Reverse Bony Bankart: avulsion of posterior glenoid labrum — posterior dislocation.

These structural lesions predispose to recurrent instability. A Hill-Sachs lesion >20% of the humeral head may engage the glenoid rim during normal range of motion (engaging Hill-Sachs), requiring operative management (Latarjet or remplissage procedure).

cards.front: What clinical tests are used to diagnose anterior vs. posterior shoulder instability?
cards.back:
Anterior instability: Apprehension test (apprehension with abduction + external rotation), Relocation test (posteriorly directed force relieves apprehension), Sulcus sign (inferior instability with distal traction). Posterior instability: Posterior apprehension/jerk test (adduct + internally rotate + posterior force causes 'jerk' sensation).

These tests are more reliably used for chronic recurrent instability than acute dislocation. The relocation test is highly specific for anterior instability when positive. The sulcus sign indicates inferior glenohumeral laxity and may suggest multidirectional instability.

cards.front: What radiographic findings distinguish anterior from posterior shoulder dislocation on AP, axillary, and trans-scapular Y views?
cards.back:
Anterior: humeral head anterior on axillary and Y views; sub-coracoid position on AP; positive rim sign (>6 mm gap between glenoid rim and humeral head). Posterior: humeral head posterior on axillary and Y ('Mercedes-Benz' sign); vacant glenoid sign on AP; 'lightbulb sign' (humeral head internally rotated appears round); reverse Hill-Sachs lesion.

The axillary view is the single most important view for diagnosing posterior dislocation — it directly visualizes the humeral head position relative to the glenoid. The 'lightbulb sign' on AP occurs because a posteriorly dislocated humerus is held in fixed internal rotation.

cards.front: What neurovascular structures must be assessed after anterior shoulder dislocation?
cards.back:
Axillary nerve: sensory patch over the deltoid ('Sergeant's Patch') and deltoid muscle contraction. Musculocutaneous nerve: sensory patch on lateral forearm and biceps contraction.

Axillary nerve injury occurs in up to 9–18% of anterior shoulder dislocations. Always document neurovascular status before and after reduction. Persistent deltoid weakness after reduction suggests axillary nerve injury and warrants EMG/nerve conduction studies.

cards.front: What x-ray view is used for evaluation of the patellofemoral joint, and what conditions is it used for?
cards.back:
Skyline (tangential) view with knees flexed at 45° — used for patella fracture, patellar dislocation, and patellofemoral syndrome.

The skyline view profiles the patella and trochlear groove in cross-section, allowing assessment of patellar tilt, trochlear dysplasia, and patellar fracture patterns. Standard AP and lateral views alone are insufficient for patellofemoral assessment.

cards.front: What is the Swimmer's view in cervical spine imaging and when is it used?
cards.back:
A lateral view taken with the arm abducted 180° to evaluate the C7-T1 junction when a standard lateral cervical spine view is inadequate to visualize this level.

The C7-T1 junction is a common site for fracture and dislocation. Failure to identify this junction on lateral cervical spine view is a significant source of missed injury. CT is now increasingly used as the primary imaging modality in high-energy trauma.

cards.front: What are the 4 joints that make up the 'shoulder complex'?
cards.back:
Glenohumeral joint, Acromioclavicular (AC) joint, Sternoclavicular (SC) joint, and Scapulothoracic joint.

All four joints work in concert for full shoulder range of motion. The glenohumeral joint provides the most mobility but is the most prone to dislocation. The scapulothoracic joint is a functional rather than true synovial joint.

cards.front: What is the normal passive range of motion of the shoulder?
cards.back:
Abduction: 180°, Adduction: 45°, Flexion: 180°, Extension: 45°, Internal rotation: to level of T4, External rotation: 45°.

Knowledge of normal shoulder ROM is essential for assessing injury or disease severity. Loss of external rotation is a key finding in posterior shoulder dislocation and adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder).

cards.front: What are the plain film findings of osteomyelitis, and when do they appear?
cards.back:
Lytic bone destruction ('moth-eaten' appearance) and periosteal reaction (formation of new bone). These findings are generally not seen until 10–12 days after onset of infection.

The delay in radiographic findings is because significant bone destruction (30–50% of bone mineral) must occur before it becomes visible on plain film. MRI is the most sensitive early modality for osteomyelitis and can detect changes within 3–5 days.

cards.front: What is a Galeazzi fracture and why is it considered a 'fracture of necessity'?
cards.back:
A Galeazzi fracture is a fracture of the distal radius with associated dislocation/disruption of the distal radioulnar joint (DRUJ). It is a 'fracture of necessity' because all cases are operative — ORIF of the radius is required, followed by assessment of DRUJ stability.

On x-ray, Galeazzi fractures show: shortening of distal radius >5 mm relative to the distal ulna, widening of DRUJ space on AP view, and dislocation of radius with respect to ulna on true lateral. If DRUJ is stable post-ORIF, splint for 10–14 days with early ROM. If unstable, ORIF or percutaneous pinning with long arm cast in supination x 2–3 weeks.

cards.front: What is a Colles' fracture and what is its classic deformity?
cards.back:
Colles' fracture is an extra-articular transverse distal radius fracture (~2 cm proximal to the radiocarpal joint) with dorsal displacement, often with ulnar styloid fracture. Classic deformity: 'dinner fork' deformity.

Most common fracture in patients >40 years, especially women with osteoporotic bone. Mechanism: FOOSH (fall on outstretched hand). X-ray findings: dorsal tilt, dorsal displacement, radial shortening, ulnar styloid fracture, radial tilt, and radial displacement. Treatment goal is to restore radial height (13 mm), radial inclination (23°), volar tilt (11°), and DRUJ stability.

cards.front: What are the general indications for surgical management of distal radius fractures?
cards.back:
Displaced intra-articular fracture, comminuted fracture, dorsal angulation >5° or volar tilt >20°, and >5 mm radial shortening.

Features of inadequate closed reduction requiring ORIF (in non-geriatric patients): radial shortening >3 mm or angulation, and intra-articular displacement/step-off >2 mm. Operative options include percutaneous pinning, external fixation, or ORIF.

cards.front: How is a Colles' fracture managed non-operatively?
cards.back:
Hematoma block (sterile, local anesthetic injected into fracture site) or conscious sedation, followed by closed reduction (traction with extension to exaggerate injury, then traction with ulnar deviation, pronation, flexion of distal fragment). Apply dorsal slab/below-elbow cast for 5–6 weeks. Obtain post-reduction films immediately; repeat x-ray weekly for first 3 weeks and at cast removal.

Operative treatment is indicated for failed closed reduction or loss of reduction. Options include percutaneous pinning, external fixation, or ORIF. Canadian guidelines follow standard orthopedic practice emphasizing restoration of radial height, inclination, and volar tilt.

cards.front: What is a Smith's fracture and how does it differ from a Colles' fracture?
cards.back:
Smith's fracture is volar displacement of the distal radius — the reverse of a Colles' fracture. Mechanism: fall onto the back of a flexed hand. Classic deformity: 'garden spade' deformity.

Non-operative treatment: closed reduction and splinting in wrist extension with hematoma or regional nerve block; long-arm cast in supination x 6 weeks. Operative treatment (ORIF) is indicated for displaced or unstable fractures.

cards.front: List early and late complications of wrist fractures.
cards.back:
Early: difficult reduction/loss of reduction, compartment syndrome, extensor pollicis longus tendon rupture, acute carpal tunnel syndrome, finger swelling with venous block, complications of tight cast/splint. Late: malunion/radial shortening, painful wrist secondary to ulnar prominence, frozen shoulder (shoulder-hand syndrome), post-traumatic arthritis, carpal tunnel syndrome, CRPS/RSD.

80% of distal radius fracture patients have normal function in 6–12 months. Most common complications are poor grip strength, stiffness, and radial shortening. Distal radius fractures in those <40 years are frequently high-energy/comminuted and more likely to require ORIF.

cards.front: What is the most common carpal bone fractured and what is its most common mechanism?
cards.back:
Scaphoid fracture is the most common carpal bone injury. Mechanism: FOOSH causing impaction of scaphoid on distal radius, most commonly resulting in a transverse fracture through the waist (65%), proximal (25%), or distal (10%) pole.

Scaphoid fractures are common in young men but not in children or elderly. They may be associated with perilunate injuries. The proximal pole receives up to 100% of its arterial blood supply from the radial artery entering at the distal pole; a proximal-third fracture disrupts this supply, leading to high AVN/nonunion risk.

cards.front: What are the clinical features of a scaphoid fracture and how should a negative initial x-ray be managed?
cards.back:
Clinical features: pain with resisted pronation, tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox, over the scaphoid tubercle, and pain with long-axis compression into the scaphoid. If the x-ray is negative but the patient has snuffbox tenderness, treat as a scaphoid fracture and repeat x-ray in 2 weeks. If still negative, order CT or MRI.

A fracture may not be radiologically visible up to 2 weeks after acute injury. The anatomical snuffbox has high sensitivity but only 20% specificity — it is also positive with many other radial-sided wrist injuries after FOOSH. CT or MRI detect occult fractures and AVN.

cards.front: What are the operative indications for scaphoid fracture, and what is the preferred surgical technique?
cards.back:
Indications: displacement ≥1 mm, comminution, interscaphoid angle >35° ('humpback' deformity), associated perilunate injury. Treatment: ORIF with buried headless compression screw.

Non-operative treatment is long-arm thumb spica cast x 4 weeks, then short-arm cast until radiographic healing (2–3 months). AVN is a major complication, especially with proximal-pole fractures. Proximal fifth fracture AVN rate approaches 100%; proximal third AVN rate is 33%; waist fractures heal 80–90%; distal pole approaches 100% healing.

cards.front: What are the specific complications of scaphoid fracture?
cards.back:
Nonunion/malunion (most common — treated with bone graft from iliac crest or distal radius with fixation); AVN of the proximal pole; delayed union (recommend surgical fixation); scaphoid nonunion advanced collapse (SNAC) — chronic nonunion leading to advanced wrist collapse and arthritis.

The proximal pole is most at risk for AVN because it receives its blood supply entirely from the distal end. Proximal-fifth fractures have nearly 100% AVN rate. SNAC wrist is analogous to SLAC (scapholunate advanced collapse) in terms of end-stage wrist arthritis pattern.

cards.front: What are the mnemonics for remembering the order of carpal bones?
cards.back:
Proximal row (lateral to medial): Scaphoid, Lunate, Triquetrum, Pisiform — 'So Long To Pinky'. Distal row (medial to lateral): Hamate, Capitate, Trapezoid, Trapezium — 'Here Comes The Thumb'.

The proximal row articulates with the distal radius and ulna. The distal row articulates with the metacarpals. This mnemonic is widely used on MCCQE1 and USMLE-style examinations.

cards.front: What are the key anatomical features of C1 and C2 vertebrae?
cards.back:
C1 (atlas): no vertebral body, no spinous process. C2 (axis): has the odontoid process (dens). There are 7 cervical vertebrae but 8 cervical nerve roots; nerve roots exit above the vertebra of the same number (e.g., C4 root exits above C4 vertebra), except C8 which exits below C7.

This anatomy has critical implications for cervical radiculopathy: nerve root compression at a given level produces motor, sensory, and reflex deficits corresponding to that level. Radiculopathy = nerve root impingement; myelopathy = spinal cord impingement.

cards.front: What are the motor, sensory, and reflex findings for C5, C6, C7, and C8 radiculopathy?
cards.back:
C5: Motor — deltoid/biceps; Sensory — axillary nerve (lateral deltoid patch); Reflex — biceps. C6: Motor — biceps/brachioradialis/wrist extension; Sensory — thumb; Reflex — biceps/brachioradialis. C7: Motor — triceps/wrist flexion/finger extension; Sensory — index and middle finger; Reflex — triceps. C8: Motor — interossei/digital flexors; Sensory — ring and little finger; Reflex — finger jerk.

Cervical radiculopathy presents with dermatomal pain, weakness in the myotome, and diminished reflex. On MCCQE1, remembering C5 = deltoid/biceps/biceps reflex, C6 = brachioradialis reflex, C7 = triceps/triceps reflex is essential.

cards.front: Describe the special tests for cervical spine pathology.
cards.back:
Compression test: pressure on head worsens radicular pain. Distraction test: traction on head relieves radicular symptoms. Valsalva test: increases intrathecal pressure, causes radicular pain. Lhermitte sign: electric shock radiating to back on forward neck flexion (MS, cervical myelopathy, B12 deficiency). Occiput-wall distance (OWD): >2 cm is abnormal, indicates thoracic hyper-kyphosis.

These tests help differentiate cervical radiculopathy from myelopathy and other neck pain etiologies. Lhermitte sign is classically associated with multiple sclerosis but can occur with any cause of cervical cord compression or B12 deficiency.

cards.front: What are the x-ray parameters to assess on a lateral cervical spine view?
cards.back:
Vertebral alignment: posterior vertebral bodies should be aligned (translation >3.5 mm is abnormal). Angulation between adjacent vertebral bodies (>11° is abnormal). Disc or facet joint widening. Anterior soft tissue space (at C3 should be <3 mm; at C4 should be <8–10 mm).

Additional cervical spine x-ray views: AP (alignment), AP odontoid (atlantoaxial articulation), oblique (pedicles and intervertebral foramina), swimmer's view (C7-T1 junction), and lateral flexion-extension views (subluxation). The anterior soft tissue space is a surrogate for retropharyngeal hematoma post-trauma.

cards.front: What are the motor, sensory, reflex, and screening test findings for L4, L5, and S1 radiculopathy?
cards.back:
L4: Motor — quadriceps (knee extension/hip flexion), tibialis anterior; Sensory — medial malleolus; Reflex — knee (patellar); Screening — squat and rise; Test — femoral stretch. L5: Motor — extensor hallucis longus, gluteus medius; Sensory — 1st dorsal webspace and lateral leg; Reflex — medial hamstring; Screening — heel walking; Test — straight leg raise. S1: Motor — peroneus longus/brevis, gastrocnemius/soleus; Sensory — lateral foot; Reflex — ankle (Achilles); Screening — walking on toes; Test — straight leg raise.

On MCCQE1, L4 = knee reflex, L5 = heel walking/EHL weakness, S1 = ankle reflex/toe walking/gastrocnemius. Disc herniation most commonly occurs at L5-S1 > L4-5 > L3-4.

cards.front: What are the special tests for lumbar spine pathology?
cards.back:
Straight leg raise (SLR): passive lifting of leg at 30–70° reproduces radicular symptoms radiating down posterior/lateral leg to knee and into foot. Lasegue maneuver: dorsiflexion of foot during SLR worsens symptoms. Femoral stretch test: with patient prone, flexing the knee and passively extending the hip reproduces anterior thigh pain (tests upper lumbar roots L2-4).

Positive contralateral SLR (pain in symptomatic leg when contralateral leg is raised) is highly specific for disc herniation. The Lasegue maneuver and Bowstring sign confirm nerve root tension. Femoral stretch tests L2, L3, and L4 nerve roots.

cards.front: What is the differential diagnosis of back pain?
cards.back:
Mechanical or nerve compression (>90%): degenerative disc/facet/ligament, disc herniation, spinal stenosis. Others (<10%): neoplastic (primary, metastatic, multiple myeloma), infectious (osteomyelitis, TB), metabolic (osteoporosis), traumatic fracture, spondyloarthropathies (ankylosing spondylitis), referred pain (aorta, renal, ureter, pancreas).

Red flags for back pain: bowel or bladder dysfunction, bilateral symptoms, constitutional symptoms/malignancy, chronic disease, paresthesias, age >50 years, IV drug use, neuromotor deficits. These require urgent investigation and possible imaging.

cards.front: How does neurogenic claudication differ from vascular claudication?
cards.back:
Neurogenic claudication: aggravated by standing/walking (walking distance variable); relieved by change in position (usually flexion, sitting, lying down); relief in ~10 minutes. Vascular claudication: aggravated by walking/exercise (reproducible); relieved by stopping walking; relief in ~2 minutes.

Neurogenic claudication is position-dependent (spinal canal widens with flexion); vascular claudication is exercise-dependent (ischemia resolves with rest). Neurogenic claudication is a hallmark of spinal stenosis. Key MCCQE1 distinction.

cards.front: What is degenerative disc disease and how is it managed?
cards.back:
Loss of vertebral disc height with age causing: bulging/tears of annulus fibrosus, change in alignment of facet joints, and osteophyte formation. Clinical features: axial back pain, pain worse with axial loading and flexion, negative straight leg raise. Non-operative: staying active with modified activity, back strengthening, NSAIDs. Do NOT use opioids; no proven efficacy for spinal traction or manipulation. Operative (rarely): decompression + fusion for severe/progressive neurological deficit or refractory cases.

Imaging (x-ray, MRI, provocative discography) is only indicated if symptoms persist >6 weeks or red flags are present. Degenerative disc disease is the most common cause of mechanical back pain. Conservative management is the cornerstone of Canadian guidelines.

cards.front: What is spinal stenosis and how is it managed?
cards.back:
Narrowing of the spinal canal — congenital (idiopathic, osteopetrosis, achondroplasia) or acquired (degenerative, iatrogenic post-surgery, ankylosing spondylosis, Paget's disease, trauma). Features: bilateral back and leg pain, neurogenic claudication, ± motor weakness. Non-operative: physiotherapy (flexion exercises, stretch/strength), NSAIDs, lumbar epidural steroids. Operative: decompressive surgery after >6 months of non-operative failure.

CT/MRI confirms narrowing of spinal canal. Neurogenic claudication is position-dependent (relieved by flexion/sitting), differentiating it from vascular claudication. Cauda equina syndrome from central compression is a surgical emergency.

cards.front: What is lumbar disc herniation and what are its clinical features?
cards.back:
Tear in annulus fibrosus allows protrusion of nucleus pulposus, most commonly at L5-S1 > L4-5 > L3-4. M:F = 3:1; only 5% become symptomatic. Clinical features: back-dominant pain (central herniation) or leg-dominant pain (lateral herniation), tenderness between spinous processes, muscle spasm, loss of lumbar lordosis, positive SLR, positive Lasegue/Bowstring, cauda equina syndrome in 1–10% (surgical emergency).

Cauda equina syndrome presents with bilateral leg weakness, saddle anesthesia, and bowel/bladder dysfunction — it is a surgical emergency requiring urgent decompression. 90% of patients improve in 3 months with non-operative treatment (extension protocol physiotherapy, NSAIDs).

cards.front: What are the operative indications for lumbar disc herniation?
cards.back:
Progressive neurological deficit, failure of symptoms to resolve within 3 months of non-operative treatment, or cauda equina syndrome due to central disc herniation. Surgical treatment: discectomy.

Non-operative treatment (extension protocol physiotherapy, NSAIDs) is first-line, with 90% improving in 3 months. Cauda equina syndrome is a surgical emergency requiring urgent discectomy. Red flags mandating urgent evaluation: bowel/bladder dysfunction, bilateral leg weakness, saddle anesthesia.

cards.front: What are the key differences between the types of low back pain in terms of aggravating factors?
cards.back:
Disc origin mechanical back pain: aggravated by flexion. Facet origin mechanical back pain: aggravated by extension, standing, and walking. Spinal stenosis: aggravated by exercise, extension, walking, and standing. Root compression/disc herniation (lateral): aggravated by flexion.

Understanding the aggravating and relieving factors helps identify the pain generator. Disc-origin pain is flexion-aggravated, facet pain is extension-aggravated, and stenosis is position-dependent (worse with extension, better with flexion). This guides treatment — extension exercises for disc herniation, flexion exercises for stenosis.

cards.front: What is spondylolysis and how is it diagnosed?
cards.back:
Spondylolysis is a defect in the pars interarticularis with no movement of the vertebral bodies. Common in athletes (gymnasts, weightlifters, backpackers, loggers). Clinical feature: activity-related back pain, pain with unilateral extension (Michelis' test). Diagnosis: oblique x-ray showing 'collar' break in the 'Scottie dog's' neck; bone scan; CT scan. Treatment: activity restriction, brace, stretching exercises.

The 'Scottie dog' sign on oblique x-ray represents the pars interarticularis as the dog's neck. A break ('collar') at this site confirms spondylolysis. Spondylolysis is distinct from spondylolisthesis, which involves actual vertebral body translation.

cards.front: What is adult isthmic spondylolisthesis and what is the Meyerding classification?
cards.back:
Spondylolisthesis is a defect in the pars interarticularis causing forward translation/slippage of one vertebra on another, usually at L5-S1. Meyerding classification by percentage of slip: Grade 1 = 0–25%, Grade 2 = 25–50%, Grade 3 = 50–75%, Grade 4 = 75–100%, Grade 5 = >100% (spondyloptosis). Mechanism: degenerative (adults), traumatic, pathological, or teratogenic.

Treatment: Grades 1–2 — symptomatic operative fusion only for intractable pain; Grades 3–5 — decompression for spondylolisthesis plus spinal fusion. Operative indications: refractory pain, progressive slip, neurological deficits, segmental instability. Complication: cauda equina syndrome from roots stretched over L5 or sacrum.

cards.front: What are the clinical features, investigations, and emergency management of a pelvic fracture?
cards.back:
Clinical features: pain, inability to bear weight, local swelling/tenderness, abnormal lower extremity positioning (external rotation), limb-length discrepancy, pelvic instability. Investigations: AP pelvis, inlet/outlet views, Judet views (acetabular fracture); CT for posterior pelvic and acetabular evaluation; assess GU injury (rectal/vaginal exam, hematuria, blood at urethral meatus — if positive, fracture is open). Emergency management: IV fluids/blood, pelvic binder/sheet, external fixation vs. emergent angiography/embolization, ± laparotomy (if FAST/DPL positive), ± pre-peritoneal packing.

Pelvic fractures carry life-threatening risk of hemorrhage. A pelvic binder reduces pelvic volume and controls bleeding in open-book fractures. Angiography with embolization addresses arterial bleeding. The 6 cardinal radiographic landmarks of the acetabulum: ilioischial line, iliopectineal line, teardrop, weight-bearing roof, posterior rim, anterior rim.

cards.front: Describe the Tile classification of pelvic fractures.
cards.back:
Type A: rotationally and vertically stable (A1 = avulsion/iliac wing fracture; A2 = minimally displaced ring fracture; A3 = transverse sacral/coccygeal fracture). Type B: rotationally unstable, vertically stable (B1 = open book/external rotation; B2 = lateral compression; B3 = bilateral). Type C: rotationally and vertically unstable (C1 = unilateral; C2 = bilateral with one side B and one side C; C3 = bilateral both type C).

Type A fractures are stable and managed non-operatively (protected weight-bearing). Operative indications include unstable pelvic ring injury, symphysis diastasis >2.5 cm, and open fractures. Complications include hemorrhage (life-threatening), GU injury, obstetrical difficulties, DVT/PE, and post-traumatic arthritis.

cards.front: What are the characteristics and treatment of posterior hip dislocation?
cards.back:
Most frequent type of hip dislocation (90%). Mechanism: severe axial load to knee with hip flexed and adducted (e.g., knee into dashboard in MVC). Clinical features: shortened, adducted, internally rotated limb. X-ray: affected femoral head appears smaller than unaffected. Treatment: urgent closed reduction under conscious sedation/GA (if no associated femoral neck fracture); ORIF if unstable or intra-articular fragments; post-reduction CT to assess congruity and fractures.

Hip dislocations should be reduced within 6 hours to decrease risk of AVN of the femoral head. Thompson and Epstein classification for posterior dislocation: Type I (no/minor acetabular wall fracture) through Type V (femoral head fracture). Hip precautions maintained for 6 weeks post-reduction.

cards.front: What is anterior hip dislocation and how does it present differently from posterior dislocation?
cards.back:
Anterior hip dislocation: mechanism — posteriorly directed axial loading with hip widely abducted and externally rotated. Two types: inferior (flexion, abduction, external rotation) and superior (extension and external rotation). Clinical features: shortened, abducted, externally rotated limb. Posterior dislocation: internally rotated, adducted. Treatment: closed reduction under conscious sedation/GA; post-reduction CT.

The limb position is key for distinguishing the two types. Anterior dislocation = external rotation and abduction; posterior dislocation = internal rotation and adduction. Up to 50% of patients with hip dislocations suffer fractures elsewhere at time of injury.

cards.front: What are the complications of hip dislocation?
cards.back:
Post-traumatic OA, AVN of femoral head (risk increases with delay in reduction), associated fractures (femoral head/neck/shaft), sciatic nerve palsy in 25% (10% permanent), heterotopic ossification (HO), thromboembolism (DVT/PE), hip instability and re-dislocation.

AVN is the most feared complication and is minimized by reducing the dislocation within 6 hours. Sciatic nerve palsy is the most common neurological complication, occurring in 25% of posterior dislocations. DVT/PE prophylaxis is essential in these patients.

cards.front: What are the clinical features of a hip fracture and what is the classic limb position?
cards.back:
Acute hip pain after a fall, inability to weight-bear, shortened and externally rotated leg, painful ROM. X-ray features of subcapital fractures: disruption of Shenton's line and altered neck-shaft angle (normal 120–130°).

Hip fractures are a major cause of morbidity and mortality in the elderly. DVT prophylaxis with LMWH (enoxaparin 40 mg SC once daily), fondaparinux, or low-dose heparin is started on admission but not within 12 hours before surgery. Early operative fixation is standard of care.

cards.front: What are the three types of hip fractures and their management?
cards.back:
Femoral neck fracture (intracapsular): x-ray AP pelvis/hip; treatment per Garden classification; complications include AVN and disruption of blood supply (medial/lateral femoral circumflex arteries). Intertrochanteric fracture (extracapsular): closed reduction under fluoroscopy then dynamic hip screw or IM nail; complications — DVT, varus displacement. Subtrochanteric fracture: closed/open reduction with IM nail; complications — malalignment, non-union, wound infection.

Intertrochanteric fractures are stable if the posteromedial cortex is intact. Subtrochanteric fractures are often high-energy in young patients and pathological in the elderly. IM nailing is the workhorse for both inter- and subtrochanteric fractures.

cards.front: Describe the Garden classification of femoral neck fractures and its treatment implications.
cards.back:
Type I: incomplete, valgus/neutral, disrupted trabeculae — internal fixation to prevent displacement (valgus impacted fracture). Type II: complete, neutral, aligned trabeculae — internal fixation. Type III: partial complete, varus, disrupted trabeculae — young: ORIF; elderly: hemi- or total hip arthroplasty. Type IV: complete, varus, disrupted trabeculae — young: ORIF; elderly: hemi- or total hip arthroplasty.

Garden III and IV fractures have high rates of AVN and nonunion, especially in the elderly, because the blood supply to the femoral head (medial and lateral femoral circumflex arteries) is disrupted. In the elderly, arthroplasty provides more reliable pain relief and faster functional recovery than ORIF.

cards.front: What are the clinical features and OA x-ray findings of hip arthritis?
cards.back:
OA: pain (groin, medial thigh) and stiffness aggravated by activity, relieved with rest; decreased ROM (internal rotation lost first); crepitus; leg length discrepancy; fixed flexion contracture (Thomas test); ± Trendelenburg sign/gait. X-ray OA findings — LOSS: Loss of joint space, Osteophytes, Subchondral sclerosis, Subchondral cysts. Inflammatory (RA) x-ray: osteopenia, periarticular erosions, concentric joint space narrowing.

Hip arthritis is managed non-operatively with weight loss, activity modification, physiotherapy, analgesics, anti-inflammatories, and walking aids. Operative management (arthroplasty) is indicated for advanced disease significantly affecting quality of life. Arthroplasty complications: component loosening, dislocation, HO, thromboembolism, infection, neurovascular injury, limb length discrepancy, periprosthetic fracture.

cards.front: What are the risk factors and mechanism for hip dislocation after total hip arthroplasty (THA)?
cards.back:
Incidence: 1–4% primary THA; 10–16% revision THA. Risk factors: post-traumatic arthritis, revision surgery, substance use, cognitive impairment (dementia), spastic/neuromuscular disease, posterior surgical approach, spinal fusion. Mechanism: posterior dislocation — flexion, adduction, internal rotation; anterior dislocation — extension and external rotation.

Hip dislocation is a common indication for early revision THA. Prevention: hip precautions (no extreme flexion, adduction, or rotation) for 6 weeks post-procedure. Closed reduction is attempted first; revision arthroplasty is indicated for recurrent dislocation.

cards.front: What is sciatica and what is its most common cause?
cards.back:
Sciatica is a symptom of radiculopathy: leg-dominant, constant, burning pain that radiates down the leg and foot. Most common cause: disc herniation.

Sciatica is distinct from mechanical back pain in that it is leg-dominant, constant, and burning, and follows a dermatomal distribution. It is caused by compression or irritation of the sciatic nerve or its contributing nerve roots (L4, L5, S1). Disc herniation is by far the most common cause, particularly at L4-5 and L5-S1.

cards.front: What red flags indicate the need for urgent imaging or surgical consultation in back pain?
cards.back:
Bowel or bladder dysfunction, bilateral symptoms, constitutional symptoms/malignancy, chronic disease, paresthesias, age >50 years, IV drug use, neuromotor deficits.

Red flags suggest serious underlying pathology such as cauda equina syndrome, malignancy, infection (osteomyelitis, TB), or abdominal aortic aneurysm. Cauda equina syndrome and ruptured aortic aneurysm are causes of acute low back pain that are surgical emergencies.

cards.front: At what spinal level does the spinal cord terminate, and what is the clinical relevance?
cards.back:
The spinal cord terminates at the conus medullaris at L1/2. Below this level, the spinal canal contains the cauda equina (individual nerve roots). Individual lumbar nerve roots exit below the pedicle of the same-numbered vertebra (e.g., L4 root exits below L4 pedicle).

This anatomical fact is critical for understanding the difference between upper motor neuron and lower motor neuron injuries in spinal pathology. Cauda equina syndrome (below L1/2) produces LMN signs, whereas cord injuries above the conus produce UMN signs. It also defines which levels can safely undergo lumbar puncture (below L1/2 = safe).

cards.front: What are the causes and mechanisms of pelvic fractures in young vs. elderly patients?
cards.back:
Young: high-energy trauma (direct or transmitted longitudinally through femur) — lateral compression, vertical shear, or anteroposterior compression fractures. Elderly: low-energy trauma (fall from standing height) — typically stable fractures managed non-operatively.

The distinction is clinically important for triage and management. High-energy pelvic fractures carry risk of life-threatening hemorrhage and associated injuries (urogenital, rectal, vascular). Elderly stable fractures are managed with protected weight-bearing and early mobilization to prevent deconditioning and DVT.

cards.front: What are the DVT prophylaxis options after elective total hip arthroplasty (THA)?
cards.back:
DOACs (e.g., rivaroxaban), ASA, heparin, or warfarin. Duration: continue for 10–35 days postoperatively.

Canadian guidelines support extended thromboprophylaxis after elective THA for 10–35 days. DOACs such as rivaroxaban are preferred for convenience and efficacy. ACCP and Canadian guidelines endorse this approach to reduce VTE risk following major lower limb arthroplasty.

cards.front: What are the operative indications for revision THA following hip dislocation?
cards.back:
Recurrent dislocations, associated polyethylene wear, malalignment, hardware failure, or infection.

After a primary closed reduction of a dislocated THA, operative revision is warranted for recurrence or mechanical failure. Infection is a particularly important cause of instability that must be excluded, as septic loosening can lead to recurrent dislocation.

cards.front: What is the most common mechanism of femoral diaphysis fracture in adults vs. children?
cards.back:
Adults: high energy trauma (MVC, fall from height, gunshot). Children: can result from low energy trauma (spiral fracture); always consider non-accidental trauma (child abuse).

Femoral shaft fractures in children from low-energy spiral mechanisms warrant consideration of non-accidental trauma (NAT). In adults, high-energy mechanisms dominate. The difference in fracture energy threshold underscores the need for child abuse awareness in pediatric fractures.

cards.front: What is the Winquist and Hansen classification used for?
cards.back:
Classification of femoral diaphysis (shaft) fractures based on degree of comminution.

The Winquist-Hansen classification grades femoral shaft fractures by comminution from Type 0 (no comminution) to Type IV (circumferential comminution). Higher grades are associated with greater instability and increased risk of complications.

cards.front: What is the preferred operative treatment for femoral shaft fractures in adults?
cards.back:
ORIF with anterograde intramedullary (IM) nail (most common). Alternatives: retrograde IM nail, plate/screw fixation, or temporary external fixation in unstable/polytrauma patients.

Antegrade IM nailing is the gold standard for femoral shaft fractures due to reliable fixation and ability for early mobilization. Retrograde nailing is used for distal fractures or when antegrade access is limited. External fixation is a damage-control measure in polytrauma.

cards.front: What percentage of femoral diaphysis fractures are associated with ipsilateral femoral neck fractures, and what is the clinical concern?
cards.back:
2–6% association with ipsilateral hip dislocation/fracture. These are reportedly missed in 19–31% of cases, making it essential to image the ipsilateral hip with every femoral shaft fracture.

Ipsilateral femoral neck fractures are commonly missed with femoral shaft fractures. Standard workup must include AP pelvis and AP/lateral hip views. Missing a femoral neck fracture can lead to avascular necrosis and significant morbidity.

cards.front: What are the three types of distal femoral fractures?
cards.back:
Extra-articular, partial articular, and complete articular fractures.

Distal femoral fractures involve the region from the articular surface to 5 cm above the metaphyseal flare. Classification by articular involvement guides treatment: extra-articular may be managed non-operatively if non-displaced; articular fractures generally require ORIF to restore joint congruity.

cards.front: What ABI threshold indicates vascular injury in a distal femoral fracture requiring angiography?
cards.back:
ABI < 0.9 is abnormal and requires angiography to evaluate for vascular injury.

The popliteal artery is at risk in distal femoral fractures. ABI is used as a screening tool; values <0.9 indicate significant vascular compromise and mandate CT angiography or formal angiography to identify injury requiring repair.

cards.front: What are the common complaints suggesting intra-articular knee pathology?
cards.back:
Locking, instability, and swelling (effusion).

Locking (inability to fully extend due to mechanical block, e.g., meniscal tear), instability (ligamentous insufficiency), and swelling (hemarthrosis/synovitis) are classic indicators of intra-articular pathology. Pseudo-locking differs — it has no mechanical block and is caused by muscle spasm or arthritis.

cards.front: Describe the Lachman test: technique, what it tests, and its diagnostic accuracy.
cards.back:
Knee held at 20–30° flexion; stabilize distal femur, attempt to anteriorly sublux tibia. Tests ACL integrity. Positive likelihood ratio: 25.0; negative likelihood ratio: 0.1 — most reliable ACL test.

The Lachman test is the most sensitive and specific bedside test for ACL injury. Less muscular stabilization at 20–30° flexion (vs. 90° for the anterior drawer test) allows better detection of anterior tibial translation. A positive test indicates ACL rupture.

cards.front: What does a positive pivot shift test indicate, and how is it performed?
cards.back:
Indicates ACL tear. Start with knee extended, internally rotate foot, slowly flex knee while applying valgus force. An incompetent ACL causes anterior tibial subluxation that reduces/externally rotates ('pivots') during flexion. PLR 25.0, NLR 0.04.

The pivot shift test demonstrates functional instability in ACL-deficient knees. It is best performed under anesthesia as it requires muscular relaxation. The clunking reduction during flexion is the 'pivot.' It is highly specific for ACL injury and useful for confirming surgical indication.

cards.front: What does the posterior sag sign indicate, and what is the mechanism of a false positive anterior drawer test in this context?
cards.back:
Posterior sag sign suggests PCL tear. Posterior tibial subluxation from the PCL tear causes the tibia to start in a posteriorly subluxed position, producing a false positive anterior drawer test as the tibia is reduced rather than truly subluxed anteriorly.

With PCL rupture, gravity causes the tibia to sag posteriorly when hips and knees are flexed at 90°.
